l: condition of rest, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 15. 1. The skilful masters (of the Tao) in old times, with a subtle
s: The condition of rest gradually arises when movement goes on.

l: fullness of self, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 15. 1. The skilful masters (of the Tao) in old times, with a subtle
s: Those who preserve this method of the Tao do not wish to be full of themselves. Through not being full of themselves, they can seem worn and not appear new and complete.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 16. 1. The (state of) vacancy should be brought to the utmost degree,
s: The unit concerns the cultivation of the state of vacancy and stillness, and the return of things to their root after their activity. It explains that this return is a fulfillment whose report is the unchanging rule. Knowing that rule produces capacity, forbearance, community of feeling, kingliness of character, likeness to heaven, and possession of the Tao. Possession of the Tao enables long endurance and freedom from bodily decay.

l: state of vacancy, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 16. 1. The (state of) vacancy should be brought to the utmost degree,
s: The state of vacancy should be brought to the utmost degree.

l: stillness, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 16. 1. The (state of) vacancy should be brought to the utmost degree,
s: Stillness should be guarded with unwearying vigour. It is the return of things to their root and may be called a reporting that they have fulfilled their appointed end.

l: things, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 16. 1. The (state of) vacancy should be brought to the utmost degree,
s: Things pass through activity and then return to their original state. In the vegetable world, after displaying luxuriant growth, they return to their root.

l: root, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 16. 1. The (state of) vacancy should be brought to the utmost degree,
s: The root is the state to which things in the vegetable world return after their luxuriant growth.

l: unchanging rule, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 16. 1. The (state of) vacancy should be brought to the utmost degree,
s: The unchanging rule is the regular report of the fulfilment of things. Knowing it is intelligence, while not knowing it leads to wild movements and evil issues.

l: knowledge of the unchanging rule, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 16. 1. The (state of) vacancy should be brought to the utmost degree,
s: Knowledge of the unchanging rule produces a grand capacity and forbearance. It leads to a community of feeling with all things.

l: community of feeling, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 16. 1. The (state of) vacancy should be brought to the utmost degree,
s: The community of feeling comes from capacity and forbearance. From it comes a kingliness of character.

l: kingliness of character, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 16. 1. The (state of) vacancy should be brought to the utmost degree,
s: Kinglyness of character arises from community of feeling. One who is king-like goes on to be heaven-like.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 16. 1. The (state of) vacancy should be brought to the utmost degree,
s: The one who becomes heaven-like possesses the Tao. Possession of the Tao enables long endurance and exemption from all danger of decay to the end of bodily life.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 17. 1. In the highest antiquity, (the people) did not know that there
s: The unit concerns the changing relationship between the people and their rulers across successive ages. The people first did not know their rulers, then loved and praised them, then feared them, and finally despised them. It says that when faith in the Tao was deficient in the rulers, a want of faith in them followed among the people. The earliest rulers acted with reticence, completed their work successfully, and left the people saying that they were as they were of themselves.

l: people, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 17. 1. In the highest antiquity, (the people) did not know that there
s: The people passed through successive attitudes toward their rulers: they first did not know them, then loved and praised them, then feared them, and finally despised them. They later said that they were as they were of themselves.

l: rulers, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 17. 1. In the highest antiquity, (the people) did not know that there
s: The rulers were regarded differently across successive ages, and a want of faith in them followed when faith in the Tao was deficient in them. The earliest rulers appeared irresolute through their reticence, completed their work successfully, and allowed the people to feel that they acted of themselves.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 17. 1. In the highest antiquity, (the people) did not know that there
s: The Tao is mentioned in connection with the rulers' faith in it. When faith in the Tao was deficient in the rulers, a want of faith in the rulers followed among the people.

l: faith (in the Tao), The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 17. 1. In the highest antiquity, (the people) did not know that there
s: When faith in the Tao was deficient in the rulers, a want of faith in the rulers ensued among the people.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 18. 1. When the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed,
s: The unit describes what happened when the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed. Benevolence and righteousness came into vogue, followed by wisdom and shrewdness, and great hypocrisy ensued. When harmony no longer prevailed throughout the six kinships, filial sons appeared; when the states and clans fell into disorder, loyal ministers appeared.

l: Great Tao (Way or Method), The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 18. 1. When the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed,
s: The Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed.

l: benevolence, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 18. 1. When the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed,
s: Benevolence came into vogue when the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed.

l: righteousness, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 18. 1. When the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed,
s: Righteousness came into vogue when the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed.

l: wisdom, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 18. 1. When the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed,
s: Wisdom appeared after benevolence and righteousness came into vogue.

l: shrewdness, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 18. 1. When the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed,
s: Shrewdness appeared after benevolence and righteousness came into vogue.

l: great hypocrisy, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 18. 1. When the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed,
s: Great hypocrisy ensued after wisdom and shrewdness appeared.

l: harmony, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 18. 1. When the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed,
s: Harmony no longer prevailed throughout the six kinships.

l: six kinships, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 18. 1. When the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed,
s: The six kinships were no longer characterized by prevailing harmony.

l: filial sons, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 18. 1. When the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed,
s: Filial sons found their manifestation when harmony no longer prevailed throughout the six kinships.

l: states and clans, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 18. 1. When the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed,
s: The states and clans fell into disorder.

l: disorder, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 18. 1. When the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed,
s: Disorder occurred in the states and clans.

l: loyal ministers, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 18. 1. When the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed,
s: Loyal ministers appeared when the states and clans fell into disorder.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 19. 1. If we could renounce our sageness and discard our wisdom, it
s: The unit concerns three proposals for governing people: renouncing sageness and wisdom, renouncing benevolence and righteousness, and renouncing artful contrivances and scheming for gain. It says that renouncing sageness and wisdom would benefit the people, while renouncing benevolence and righteousness would restore filial and kindly behavior. It also says that abandoning artful contrivances and scheming for gain would eliminate thieves and robbers. The three methods are associated with olden ways that failed in elegance, while simple and plain courses would avoid selfish ends and many lusts.

l: people, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 19. 1. If we could renounce our sageness and discard our wisdom, it
s: The people would benefit greatly if sageness and wisdom were renounced. They would again become filial and kindly if benevolence and righteousness were discarded.

l: sageness, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 19. 1. If we could renounce our sageness and discard our wisdom, it
s: Sageness is presented as something that should be renounced for the people’s benefit.

l: wisdom, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 19. 1. If we could renounce our sageness and discard our wisdom, it
s: Wisdom is presented as something that should be discarded for the people’s benefit.

l: methods of government, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 19. 1. If we could renounce our sageness and discard our wisdom, it
s: The three methods of government concern renouncing sageness and wisdom, benevolence and righteousness, and artful contrivances and scheming for gain. They are said to have thought olden ways failed in elegance and used names to veil their lack of worth, whereas simple, plain, and true courses would avoid selfish ends and many lusts.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 20.
s: The unit contrasts renouncing learning with the apparent troubles and distinctions that arise among people. It presents the speaker as unlike the multitude of men, who seem satisfied, capable, and well supplied, while the speaker appears listless, confused, homeless, and lacking a sphere of action. The speaker nevertheless values the nursing-mother, the Tao. The text also says that what all men fear is feared, and that questions asking to be discussed have a wide and endless range.

l: learning, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 20.
s: Learning is presented as something that can be renounced, with the claim that renouncing it brings no troubles.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 20.
s: The Tao is called the nursing-mother, and the speaker values it.

l: speaker (the 'I'), The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 20.
s: The speaker appears listless, still, dejected, forlorn, and without desires that have shown themselves. The speaker feels unlike other men, with a stupid and chaotic mind, seeming dull, confused, incapable, and without a place to rest, but values the Tao.

l: men in general, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 20.
s: Men in general are described as fearing what is indeed to be feared. They are also contrasted with the speaker, appearing bright, intelligent, discriminating, and engaged in spheres of action.

l: multitude of men, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 20.
s: The multitude of men look satisfied and pleased, as if enjoying a full banquet or standing on a tower in spring. They seem to have enough and to spare, unlike the speaker.

l: fear, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 20.
s: Fear is described as something all men experience: what all men fear is indeed to be feared.

l: questions, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 20.
s: Questions are described as asking to be discussed, and their range is said to be wide and without end.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 21.
s: The unit concerns Tao as the source of the grandest forms of active force. Tao eludes sight and touch, yet contains the forms, semblances, and essences of all things. Its essences enfold the truth of what will later be seen, and Tao's name passes not away. The text attributes the enduring beauty and lack of decay in existing things to the nature of the Tao.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 21.
s: Tao is the source of the grandest forms of active force. It eludes sight and touch, contains the forms, semblances, and essences of things, and does not pass away.

l: active force, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 21.
s: Active force comes from Tao, which is its only source.

l: things, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 21.
s: The forms, semblances, and essences of things are contained in Tao. Things form in beautiful array and do not know decay.

l: nature of the Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 21.
s: The nature of the Tao explains how the beauties of existing things endure and remain without decay.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 22. 1. The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty,
s: The unit explains that what is partial, crooked, empty, or worn out can become complete, straight, full, or new. It concerns a person with few or many desires and the sage, who embraces humility and avoids self-display, self-assertion, self-boasting, and self-complacency. The sage thereby gains recognition and superiority, and no one in the world can strive with him. It teaches that the saying about the partial becoming complete comprehends all real completion.

l: sage, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 22. 1. The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty,
s: The sage embraces the one thing of humility and manifests it to all the world. By avoiding self-display, self-assertion, self-boasting, self-complacency, and striving, he shines, is distinguished, receives acknowledgment of his merit, acquires superiority, and cannot be opposed in striving by anyone in the world.

l: completion, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 22. 1. The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty,
s: Completion is described as the partial becoming complete, the crooked becoming straight, the empty becoming full, and the worn out becoming new. All real completion is comprehended under this saying.

l: desires, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 22. 1. The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty,
s: A person whose desires are few gets them, while a person whose desires are many goes astray.

l: world, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 22. 1. The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty,
s: The sage manifests humility to all the world. No one in the world is able to strive with him.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 23. 1. Abstaining from speech marks him who is obeying the spontaneity
s: The unit concerns abstaining from speech, the spontaneity of nature, and the Tao. It says that Heaven and Earth cannot sustain violent or sudden actions for long, and therefore man cannot either. A person making the Tao his business agrees with people according to whether they pursue the Tao, pursue its manifestation, or fail in both, and such agreement brings happiness of attaining to the Tao; insufficient faith causes a lack of faith in him.

l: Heaven, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 23. 1. Abstaining from speech marks him who is obeying the spontaneity
s: Heaven contributes to violent wind and sudden rain, but cannot make such spasmodic actings last long.

l: Earth, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 23. 1. Abstaining from speech marks him who is obeying the spontaneity
s: Earth contributes to violent wind and sudden rain, but cannot make such spasmodic actings last long.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 23. 1. Abstaining from speech marks him who is obeying the spontaneity
s: The Tao is what a person may make his business and what people may pursue. Agreement with the Tao brings the happiness of attaining to it.

l: manifestation of the Tao's course, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 23. 1. Abstaining from speech marks him who is obeying the spontaneity
s: The manifestation of the Tao's course is an object that people may make their pursuit. Agreement concerning it brings the happiness of attaining to the Tao.

l: person making the Tao his business, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 23. 1. Abstaining from speech marks him who is obeying the spontaneity
s: The person making the Tao his business agrees with people according to whether they pursue the Tao, pursue its manifestation, or fail in both. When he lacks sufficient faith, a lack of faith in him ensues among the others.

l: people pursuing the Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 23. 1. Abstaining from speech marks him who is obeying the spontaneity
s: People pursuing the Tao agree with the person making the Tao his business in the Tao. They have the happiness of attaining to it.

l: people making the manifestation of the Tao's course their object, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 23. 1. Abstaining from speech marks him who is obeying the spontaneity
s: People making the manifestation of the Tao's course their object agree with the person making the Tao his business in that manifestation. They have the happiness of attaining to the Tao.

l: happiness of attaining to the Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 23. 1. Abstaining from speech marks him who is obeying the spontaneity
s: The happiness of attaining to the Tao is received by those who agree in the Tao, agree in its manifestation, or agree in their failure.

l: faith (in the Tao), The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 23. 1. Abstaining from speech marks him who is obeying the spontaneity
s: Faith must be sufficient on the part of the person making the Tao his business. When it is not sufficient, a lack of faith in him ensues on the part of the others.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 24. He who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm; he who stretches
s: The unit concerns a person who displays himself, asserts his own views, vaunts himself, or is self-conceited. It says that such a person does not shine, is not distinguished, does not have his merit acknowledged, and is not allowed superiority. It compares these conditions, from the standpoint of the Tao, to remnants of food or a tumour on the body, which all dislike. Those who pursue the course of the Tao therefore do not adopt or allow them.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 24. He who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm; he who stretches
s: The Tao provides the standpoint from which self-display, self-assertion, vaunting, and self-conceit are judged. From this standpoint, such conditions are like remnants of food or a tumour on the body, which all dislike.

l: person (the one who displays himself, asserts his own views, vaunts himself, or is self-conceited), The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 24. He who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm; he who stretches
s: The person who displays himself does not shine, and the person who asserts his own views is not distinguished. The person who vaunts himself does not have his merit acknowledged, and the self-conceited person is not allowed superiority.

l: those who pursue the course of the Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 24. He who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm; he who stretches
s: Those who pursue the course of the Tao do not adopt or allow the conditions associated with self-display, self-assertion, vaunting, or self-conceit.

l: conditions of self-display and self-assertion, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 24. He who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm; he who stretches
s: The conditions of self-display and self-assertion are viewed from the standpoint of the Tao as like remnants of food or a tumour on the body, which all dislike. Those who pursue the course of the Tao do not adopt or allow them.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 25. 1. There was something undefined and complete, coming into
s: The passage describes something undefined and complete that existed before Heaven and Earth and is regarded as the Mother of all things. It names this thing the Tao and calls it The Great, saying that it passes on, becomes remote, and returns. Tao, Heaven, Earth, and the sage king are identified as the four great things in the universe. Man follows the law of the Earth, the Earth follows Heaven, Heaven follows the Tao, and the Tao follows its own nature.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 25. 1. There was something undefined and complete, coming into
s: The Tao is the name given to something undefined and complete that existed before Heaven and Earth and is regarded as the Mother of all things. It is called The Great, passes on, becomes remote, returns, and follows its own nature.

l: Heaven, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 25. 1. There was something undefined and complete, coming into
s: Heaven is one of the four great things in the universe. It takes its law from the Tao.

l: Earth, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 25. 1. There was something undefined and complete, coming into
s: Earth is one of the four great things in the universe. It takes its law from Heaven.

l: sage king, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 25. 1. There was something undefined and complete, coming into
s: The sage king is one of the four great things in the universe.

l: Man, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 25. 1. There was something undefined and complete, coming into
s: Man takes his law from the Earth.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 26. 1. Gravity is the root of lightness; stillness, the ruler of
s: The passage teaches that gravity is the root of lightness and stillness rules movement. A wise prince traveling all day stays near his baggage waggons and remains indifferent to brilliant prospects. The lord of a myriad chariots must not act lightly before the kingdom, because doing so loses his root of gravity, while active movement causes him to lose his throne.

l: gravity, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 26. 1. Gravity is the root of lightness; stillness, the ruler of
s: Gravity is the root of lightness.

l: lightness, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 26. 1. Gravity is the root of lightness; stillness, the ruler of
s: Lightness is rooted in gravity. If the lord of a myriad chariots acts lightly before the kingdom, he loses his root of gravity.

l: stillness, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 26. 1. Gravity is the root of lightness; stillness, the ruler of
s: Stillness is the ruler of movement.

l: movement, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 26. 1. Gravity is the root of lightness; stillness, the ruler of
s: Movement is ruled by stillness. If the lord of a myriad chariots proceeds to active movement, he loses his throne.

l: wise prince, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 26. 1. Gravity is the root of lightness; stillness, the ruler of
s: The wise prince, marching the whole day, stays near his baggage waggons and remains indifferent to brilliant prospects.

l: kingdom, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 26. 1. Gravity is the root of lightness; stillness, the ruler of
s: The kingdom is the realm before which the lord of a myriad chariots must not carry himself lightly.

l: throne, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 26. 1. Gravity is the root of lightness; stillness, the ruler of
s: The throne is lost by the lord of a myriad chariots if he proceeds to active movement.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 27. 1. The skilful traveller leaves no traces of his wheels or
s: The unit describes the skilful traveller, speaker, reckoner, closer, and binder as acting without leaving traces, faults, tallies, bolts, bars, strings, or knots. It says that the sage skilfully saves every man and thing, casting none away, which is called “Hiding the light of his procedure.” It presents the man of skill as a master to the person without skill, and the person without skill as helper of the man of skill’s reputation; this relationship is called “The utmost degree of mystery.”

l: sage, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 27. 1. The skilful traveller leaves no traces of his wheels or
s: The sage is always skilful at saving men and things, so he does not cast away any man or anything.

l: man of skill, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 27. 1. The skilful traveller leaves no traces of his wheels or
s: The man of skill is a master to be looked up to by the person without skill. He is helped by the reputation of the person without skill, who serves as his helper.

l: person without skill, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 27. 1. The skilful traveller leaves no traces of his wheels or
s: The person without skill looks up to the man of skill as a master. He serves as a helper of the reputation of the man of skill.

l: skill, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 27. 1. The skilful traveller leaves no traces of his wheels or
s: Skill is shown in acting without traces, faults, tallies, bolts, bars, strings, or knots, and in saving men and things without casting them away.

l: Hiding the light (of his procedure), The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 27. 1. The skilful traveller leaves no traces of his wheels or
s: “Hiding the light of his procedure” is the name given to the sage’s skilful saving of every man and thing without casting anything away.

l: The utmost degree of mystery, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 27. 1. The skilful traveller leaves no traces of his wheels or
s: “The utmost degree of mystery” describes the relationship in which the man of skill is honoured as a master and the person without skill serves as his helper.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 28.
s: The unit describes three ways of preserving constant excellence: knowing strength while maintaining feebleness, knowing whiteness while remaining in black's shade, and knowing glory while accepting disgrace. Each way leads to simplicity, humility, or the state of the simple infant, with return to man's first state. It then states that the unwrought material, when divided, forms vessels, and that the sage, when employed, becomes the Head of all the Officers and governs without violent measures.

l: sage, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 28.
s: When employed, the sage becomes the Head of all the Officers of government. In the greatest regulations, the sage employs no violent measures.

l: constant excellence, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 28.
s: Constant excellence is retained by one who knows his manhood's strength yet maintains female feebleness, displayed by one who knows how white attracts yet remains within black's shade, and completed by one who knows how glory shines yet loves disgrace.

l: the simple child (the sage), The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 28.
s: The simple child is the state reached by maintaining strength with feebleness, and the simple infant man is found in the one who accepts disgrace.

l: man's first state, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 28.
s: Man's first state is returned to by the one who knows how white attracts yet remains within black's shade.

l: the unwrought material, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 28.
s: When divided and distributed, the unwrought material forms vessels.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 29. 1. If any one should wish to get the kingdom for himself, and to
s: The unit concerns a person who wishes to gain the kingdom through active deeds. It teaches that the kingdom is spirit-like, cannot be obtained by forceful action, and is destroyed by trying to win it or lost by trying to hold it. It describes the course and nature of things as reversing what was ahead and turning strength into weakness, after which the sage rejects excessive effort, extravagance, and easy indulgence.

l: person (the one who would get the kingdom), The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 29. 1. If any one should wish to get the kingdom for himself, and to
s: The person wishes to get the kingdom for himself by what he does, but he will not succeed. By trying to win the kingdom through active doing, he destroys it; by trying to hold it, he loses it.

l: kingdom, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 29. 1. If any one should wish to get the kingdom for himself, and to
s: The kingdom is described as a spirit-like thing that cannot be obtained by active doing. Attempts to win it destroy it, and attempts to hold it cause it to be lost.

l: course and nature of things, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 29. 1. If any one should wish to get the kingdom for himself, and to
s: The course and nature of things causes what was in front to become behind and what was warm to become freezing. It also shows strength becoming the spoil of weakness and stored resources being mocked by ruins.

l: sage, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 29. 1. If any one should wish to get the kingdom for himself, and to
s: The sage puts away excessive effort, extravagance, and easy indulgence.

l: excessive effort, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 29. 1. If any one should wish to get the kingdom for himself, and to
s: The sage puts away excessive effort.

l: extravagance, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 29. 1. If any one should wish to get the kingdom for himself, and to
s: The sage puts away extravagance.

l: easy indulgence, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 29. 1. If any one should wish to get the kingdom for himself, and to
s: The sage puts away easy indulgence.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 30. 1. He who would assist a lord of men in harmony with the Tao will
s: The unit concerns He who would assist a lord of men in harmony with the Tao and how he should act in the kingdom. He should not assert mastery by force of arms, because such action brings a proper return, and wherever a host is stationed, briars and thorns spring up. A skilful commander strikes a decisive blow and stops, guarding against vanity, boastfulness, arrogance, and the desire for mastery. Things that reach strong maturity become old, and what is not in accordance with the Tao soon comes to an end.

l: He who would assist a lord of men in harmony with the Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 30. 1. He who would assist a lord of men in harmony with the Tao will
s: He does not assert his mastery in the kingdom by force of arms. He strikes only from necessity, stops after a decisive blow, and guards against vanity, boastfulness, arrogance, and the wish for mastery.

l: lord of men, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 30. 1. He who would assist a lord of men in harmony with the Tao will
s: The lord of men is the one whom He who would assist a lord of men in harmony with the Tao would assist.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 30. 1. He who would assist a lord of men in harmony with the Tao will
s: The Tao is the standard with which conduct is compared. What is not in accordance with the Tao soon comes to an end.

l: kingdom, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 30. 1. He who would assist a lord of men in harmony with the Tao will
s: The kingdom is where mastery must not be asserted by force of arms.

l: mastery, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 30. 1. He who would assist a lord of men in harmony with the Tao will
s: Mastery is not to be asserted through force of arms or continued operations. The skilful commander avoids completing mastery out of a wish for it.

l: host, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 30. 1. He who would assist a lord of men in harmony with the Tao will
s: Wherever a host is stationed, briars and thorns spring up.

l: sequence of great armies, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 30. 1. He who would assist a lord of men in harmony with the Tao will
s: In the sequence of great armies there are sure to be bad years.

l: great armies, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 30. 1. He who would assist a lord of men in harmony with the Tao will
s: Great armies are associated with a sequence in which there are sure to be bad years.

l: skilful commander, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 30. 1. He who would assist a lord of men in harmony with the Tao will
s: The skilful commander strikes a decisive blow and stops. He does not continue operations to assert and complete mastery, and he remains on guard against vanity, boastfulness, and arrogance.

l: decisive blow, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 30. 1. He who would assist a lord of men in harmony with the Tao will
s: The decisive blow is struck by a skilful commander, who then stops. It is struck as a matter of necessity, not from a wish for mastery.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 31. 1. Now arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen,
s: The unit concerns arms, those who have the Tao, and the superior man’s attitude toward war and victory. Arms are described as instruments of evil omen that the superior man uses only when necessity compels him. Victory by force is undesirable because delighting in the slaughter of men prevents a person from getting his will in the kingdom. The unit also explains how left and right positions relate to festivity, mourning, military command, and rites of mourning.

l: arms, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 31. 1. Now arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen,
s: Arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen and are hateful to all creatures. The superior man uses them only when compelled by necessity and does not prize victory achieved through them.

l: those who have the Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 31. 1. Now arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen,
s: Those who have the Tao do not like to employ arms.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 31. 1. Now arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen,
s: The Tao is associated with those who do not like to employ arms.

l: superior man, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 31. 1. Now arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen,
s: The superior man ordinarily considers the left hand the most honourable place, but in time of war he considers the right hand so. He does not regard sharp weapons as his instruments, uses them only from necessity, prizes calm and repose, and does not desire victory by force.

l: war, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 31. 1. Now arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen,
s: In time of war, the right hand is the superior man’s place. The second in command is placed on the left, while the general commanding in chief is placed on the right as in the rites of mourning.

l: victory, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 31. 1. Now arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen,
s: Victory by force of arms is undesirable to the superior man. To consider it desirable is to delight in the slaughter of men.

l: slaughter of men, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 31. 1. Now arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen,
s: Delighting in the slaughter of men prevents a person from getting his will in the kingdom. He who has killed multitudes of men should weep for them with the bitterest grief.

l: kingdom, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 31. 1. Now arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen,
s: A person who delights in the slaughter of men cannot get his will in the kingdom.

l: mourning, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 31. 1. Now arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen,
s: On occasions of mourning, the right hand is the prized position. The general commanding in chief has his place on the right, according to the rites of mourning.

l: rites of mourning, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 31. 1. Now arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen,
s: The rites of mourning assign the right-hand position to the general commanding in chief. The victor in battle has his place rightly according to those rites.

l: battle, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 31. 1. Now arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen,
s: The victor in battle has his place according to the rites of mourning. He who has killed multitudes of men should grieve for them with the bitterest grief.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 32. 1. The Tao, considered as unchanging, has no name.
s: The unit concerns the Tao and its relation to the whole world. The Tao, in its unchanging primordial simplicity, has no name, but when it acts it acquires a name that allows people to know where to rest and avoid failure and error. If a feudal prince or king could guard and hold it, all would spontaneously submit to him. Heaven and Earth, under its guidance, unite and send down sweet dew without human direction, and the Tao relates to the world as great rivers and seas relate to valley streams.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 32. 1. The Tao, considered as unchanging, has no name.
s: The Tao is considered unchanging and without a name in its primordial simplicity. When it proceeds to action, it acquires a name that enables people to know where to rest and avoid failure and error. It guides Heaven and Earth and relates to the whole world as great rivers and seas relate to valley streams.

l: the world, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 32. 1. The Tao, considered as unchanging, has no name.
s: The whole world dares not deal with the Tao in its primordial simplicity as a minister. If a feudal prince or king could guard and hold the Tao, the whole world would spontaneously submit to him.

l: feudal prince or king, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 32. 1. The Tao, considered as unchanging, has no name.
s: A feudal prince or king who could guard and hold the Tao would receive the spontaneous submission of all.

l: Heaven and Earth, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 32. 1. The Tao, considered as unchanging, has no name.
s: Heaven and Earth, under the Tao's guidance, unite together and send down sweet dew. The sweet dew reaches equally everywhere without the directions of men.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 33. 1. He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is
s: The unit contrasts knowledge of other men with knowledge of oneself, calling the former discernment and the latter intelligence. It says that overcoming others is strength, while overcoming oneself is might. It describes satisfaction with one's lot as wealth and continued energetic action as evidence of a firm will. It adds that fulfilling the requirements of one's position leads to continuance, while dying without perishing constitutes longevity.

l: other men, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 33. 1. He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is
s: Knowing other men is described as discernment.

l: self, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 33. 1. He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is
s: Knowing oneself is described as intelligence. Overcoming oneself is described as might.

l: others, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 33. 1. He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is
s: Overcoming others is described as strength.

l: lot, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 33. 1. He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is
s: Being satisfied with one's lot is described as being rich.

l: energy, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 33. 1. He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is
s: Acting with energy is associated with continuing to act.

l: will, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 33. 1. He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is
s: Continuing to act with energy is said to indicate a firm will.

l: death, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 33. 1. He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is
s: Death is presented as occurring without necessarily resulting in perishing.

l: perishing, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 33. 1. He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is
s: Not perishing after death is associated with longevity.

l: longevity, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 33. 1. He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is
s: Longevity is attributed to dying without perishing.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 34. 1. All-pervading is the Great Tao! It may be found on the left
s: The unit concerns the Great Tao, all things, and the sage. The Great Tao is everywhere, produces all things without claiming authority, and presides over their return to their root. All things depend on it, obey it, and do not know that it governs their actions. The sage accomplishes great achievements by not making himself great.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 34. 1. All-pervading is the Great Tao! It may be found on the left
s: The Great Tao is all-pervading and may be found on the left hand and on the right. It produces and clothes all things without claiming credit or lordship, and it presides over their return to their root.

l: all things, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 34. 1. All-pervading is the Great Tao! It may be found on the left
s: All things depend on the Great Tao for their production and obey it. They return to their root and disappear without knowing that the Great Tao presides over their doing so.

l: sage, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 34. 1. All-pervading is the Great Tao! It may be found on the left
s: The sage is able to accomplish great achievements by not making himself great.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 35. 1. To him who holds in his hands the Great Image (of the invisible
s: The unit concerns him who holds the Great Image of the invisible Tao in his hands. The whole world repairs itself around him, and men resort to him without hurt, finding rest, peace, and ease. Music and dainties can make a passing guest stop briefly, but the Tao seems insipid, without flavour, and not worth looking at or listening to. Despite this appearance, the use of the Tao is inexhaustible.

l: holder of the Great Image, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 35. 1. To him who holds in his hands the Great Image (of the invisible
s: He holds the Great Image of the invisible Tao in his hands. The whole world repairs around him, and men resort to him without hurt, finding rest, peace, and ease.

l: Great Image, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 35. 1. To him who holds in his hands the Great Image (of the invisible
s: The Great Image is held in the hands of him who holds the invisible Tao. The unit associates it with the repair of the whole world and with rest, peace, and ease for men.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 35. 1. To him who holds in his hands the Great Image (of the invisible
s: The Tao is described as coming from the mouth, yet seeming insipid, without flavour, and not worth looking at or listening to. Its use is nevertheless inexhaustible.

l: the world, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 35. 1. To him who holds in his hands the Great Image (of the invisible
s: The whole world repairs itself around him who holds the Great Image of the invisible Tao.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 36. 1. When one is about to take an inspiration, he is sure to make a
s: The unit describes a procedure called 'Hiding the light (of his procedure).' It explains that weakening follows strengthening, overthrowing follows raising up, and despoiling follows making gifts. It states that the soft overcomes the hard and the weak overcomes the strong. It also says that fishes should not be taken from the deep and that instruments for the profit of a state should not be shown to the people.

l: Hiding the light (of his procedure), The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 36. 1. When one is about to take an inspiration, he is sure to make a
s: Hiding the light (of his procedure) is the practice of first making an expiration before taking an inspiration, strengthening before weakening, raising up before overthrowing, and making gifts before despoiling.

l: the soft, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 36. 1. When one is about to take an inspiration, he is sure to make a
s: The soft overcomes the hard.

l: the hard, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 36. 1. When one is about to take an inspiration, he is sure to make a
s: The hard is overcome by the soft.

l: the weak, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 36. 1. When one is about to take an inspiration, he is sure to make a
s: The weak overcomes the strong.

l: strength, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 36. 1. When one is about to take an inspiration, he is sure to make a
s: The strong is overcome by the weak.

l: fishes, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 36. 1. When one is about to take an inspiration, he is sure to make a
s: Fishes should not be taken from the deep.

l: instruments for the profit of a state, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 36. 1. When one is about to take an inspiration, he is sure to make a
s: Instruments for the profit of a state should not be shown to the people.

l: state, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 36. 1. When one is about to take an inspiration, he is sure to make a
s: The state is associated with instruments for its profit, which should not be shown to the people.

l: people, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 36. 1. When one is about to take an inspiration, he is sure to make a
s: The people should not be shown instruments for the profit of a state.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 37. 1. The Tao in its regular course does nothing (for the sake of
s: The unit concerns the Tao, princes and kings, and the effects of maintaining the Tao. The Tao does nothing for the sake of doing it, and therefore there is nothing it does not do. If princes and kings maintained the Tao, all things would transform themselves through them. The speaker says that if this transformation became an object of desire, the desire would be expressed through nameless simplicity, which is free from external aims and allows all things to proceed as they will.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 37. 1. The Tao in its regular course does nothing (for the sake of
s: The Tao in its regular course does nothing for the sake of doing it, and so there is nothing which it does not do. If princes and kings maintained it, all things would of themselves be transformed by them.

l: all things, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 37. 1. The Tao in its regular course does nothing (for the sake of
s: All things would of themselves be transformed if princes and kings were able to maintain the Tao. With no desire, all things go right as of their own will.

l: transformation, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 37. 1. The Tao in its regular course does nothing (for the sake of
s: The transformation of all things through princes and kings could become an object of desire to the speaker.

l: desire, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 37. 1. The Tao in its regular course does nothing (for the sake of
s: If the transformation became an object of desire, the speaker would express the desire by the nameless simplicity. With no desire, there is rest and stillness.

l: nameless simplicity, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 37. 1. The Tao in its regular course does nothing (for the sake of
s: The nameless simplicity is the expression of desire for the transformation. Simplicity without a name is free from all external aim.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, PART II. / 38. 1. (Those who) possessed in highest degree the attributes (of the
s: The unit concerns those who possess the attributes of the Tao, benevolence, righteousness, and propriety, and the Great man. It contrasts the highest and lower degrees of possessing these qualities, especially whether they act without purpose or constantly seek to display and carry them out. It describes propriety as an attenuated form of leal-heartedness and good faith and as the beginning of disorder, while swift apprehension is a flower of the Tao and the beginning of stupidity. The Great man abides by what is solid and chooses the fruit over the flower.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, PART II. / 38. 1. (Those who) possessed in highest degree the attributes (of the
s: When the Tao is lost, its attributes appear. Swift apprehension is described as a flower of the Tao and the beginning of stupidity.

l: benevolence, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, PART II. / 38. 1. (Those who) possessed in highest degree the attributes (of the
s: When the attributes of the Tao are lost, benevolence appears. Those who possess the highest benevolence are always seeking to carry it out and have no need to be doing so.

l: righteousness, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, PART II. / 38. 1. (Those who) possessed in highest degree the attributes (of the
s: When benevolence is lost, righteousness appears. Those who possess the highest righteousness are always seeking to carry it out and have need to be so doing.

l: propriety, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, PART II. / 38. 1. (Those who) possessed in highest degree the attributes (of the
s: When righteousness is lost, propriety appears. Propriety is the attenuated form of leal-heartedness and good faith and is also the commencement of disorder; those who possess it in the highest degree seek to show it, and when men do not respond, they bare the arm and march up to them.

l: Great man, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, PART II. / 38. 1. (Those who) possessed in highest degree the attributes (of the
s: The Great man abides by what is solid and eschews what is flimsy. He dwells with the fruit and not with the flower, putting away the one and choosing the other.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 39. 1. The things which from of old have got the One (the Tao) are--
s: The unit concerns the One (the Tao) and the things that receive their qualities from it. Heaven becomes bright and pure, Earth firm and sure, spirits powerful, valleys full, and creatures alive through the One (Tao). Princes and kings receive from it the model they give to all, but without moral sway they decay. The text teaches that dignity and loftiness depend on humble foundations, which princes and kings acknowledge by calling themselves lowly names.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 39. 1. The things which from of old have got the One (the Tao) are--
s: The One (Tao) gives Heaven brightness and purity, Earth firmness and certainty, spirits their powers, valleys their fullness, and creatures their life. Princes and kings receive from it the model they give to all.

l: Heaven, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 39. 1. The things which from of old have got the One (the Tao) are--
s: Heaven is bright and pure through the One (Tao). If it were not pure, it would soon rend.

l: Earth, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 39. 1. The things which from of old have got the One (the Tao) are--
s: Earth is firm and sure through the One (Tao). If it were not sure, it would break and bend.

l: spirits, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 39. 1. The things which from of old have got the One (the Tao) are--
s: Spirits receive powers through the One (Tao). Without those powers, they would soon fail.

l: valleys, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 39. 1. The things which from of old have got the One (the Tao) are--
s: Valleys are kept full throughout their void through the One (Tao). Without that fullness, drought would parch each vale.

l: creatures, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 39. 1. The things which from of old have got the One (the Tao) are--
s: Creatures live through the One (Tao). Without that life, they would pass away.

l: princes, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 39. 1. The things which from of old have got the One (the Tao) are--
s: Princes and kings receive from the One (Tao) the model they give to all. Without moral sway, they would decay despite being grand and high, so they call themselves 'Orphans,' 'Men of small virtue,' and 'Carriages without a nave.'

l: dignity, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 39. 1. The things which from of old have got the One (the Tao) are--
s: Dignity finds its firm root in its previous meanness. Princes and kings acknowledge this foundation when they consider themselves mean.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 40.
s: The unit describes the movement and workings of the Tao. It says the Tao proceeds through contraries, with weakness marking the course of its mighty deeds. All things under heaven sprang from the Tao as existing and named. Existence sprang from the Tao as non-existent and not named.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 40.
s: The Tao proceeds by contraries, and weakness marks the course of its mighty deeds. All things under heaven sprang from it as existing and named, while existence sprang from it as non-existent and not named.

l: all things under heaven, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 40.
s: All things under heaven sprang from the Tao as existing and named.

l: existence, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 40.
s: Existence sprang from the Tao as non-existent and not named.

l: non-existence, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 40.
s: Non-existence is presented as the state from which existence sprang, and as not named.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 41. 1. Scholars of the highest class, when they hear about the Tao,
s: The unit concerns the Tao and how different classes of scholars respond when they hear about it. Scholars of the highest class earnestly practice the Tao, while middle-class scholars alternate between keeping and losing it, and lowest-class scholars laugh at it. The text describes the Tao through paradoxes, portraying it as hidden, nameless, difficult to perceive, and associated with humility, simplicity, and incompleteness. Despite being hidden and nameless, the Tao skilfully imparts what all things need and brings them to completion.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 41. 1. Scholars of the highest class, when they hear about the Tao,
s: The Tao is presented through paradoxical descriptions: it may seem lacking in brightness, involve apparent retreat, resemble a rugged track, and appear humble, incomplete, or changeable. It is hidden and has no name, yet it skilfully imparts to all things what they need and makes them complete.

l: scholars (highest class), The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 41. 1. Scholars of the highest class, when they hear about the Tao,
s: When scholars of the highest class hear about the Tao, they earnestly carry it into practice.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 42. 1. The Tao produced One; One produced Two; Two produced Three;
s: The Tao produces One, One produces Two, and Two produces Three, while Three produces All things. All things leave behind Obscurity, move toward Brightness, and are harmonised by the Breath of Vacancy. Men dislike being orphans, having little virtue, or being carriages without naves, although kings and princes use these designations for themselves. The text teaches that some things are increased by being diminished, that violent and strong do not die their natural death, and that this is the basis of the teaching.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 42. 1. The Tao produced One; One produced Two; Two produced Three;
s: The Tao produced One.

l: One, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 42. 1. The Tao produced One; One produced Two; Two produced Three;
s: One was produced by the Tao and produced Two.

l: Two, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 42. 1. The Tao produced One; One produced Two; Two produced Three;
s: Two was produced by One and produced Three.

l: Three, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 42. 1. The Tao produced One; One produced Two; Two produced Three;
s: Three was produced by Two and produced All things.

l: all things, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 42. 1. The Tao produced One; One produced Two; Two produced Three;
s: All things leave behind the Obscurity out of which they have come and go forward to embrace the Brightness into which they have emerged. They are harmonised by the Breath of Vacancy.

l: Obscurity, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 42. 1. The Tao produced One; One produced Two; Two produced Three;
s: Obscurity is what All things leave behind, and it is where they have come from.

l: Brightness, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 42. 1. The Tao produced One; One produced Two; Two produced Three;
s: Brightness is what All things go forward to embrace, and it is where they have emerged.

l: Breath of Vacancy, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 42. 1. The Tao produced One; One produced Two; Two produced Three;
s: The Breath of Vacancy harmonises All things.

l: men, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 42. 1. The Tao produced One; One produced Two; Two produced Three;
s: Men dislike being orphans, having little virtue, and being as carriages without naves. Men are taught that some things are increased by being diminished and others are diminished by being increased.

l: violent and strong, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 42. 1. The Tao produced One; One produced Two; Two produced Three;
s: The violent and strong do not die their natural death. Their fate is made the basis of the teaching.

l: natural death, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 42. 1. The Tao produced One; One produced Two; Two produced Three;
s: The violent and strong do not die their natural death.

l: teaching, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 42. 1. The Tao produced One; One produced Two; Two produced Three;
s: The teaching says that some things are increased by being diminished and others are diminished by being increased. It also takes the fact that the violent and strong do not die their natural death as its basis.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 43. 1. The softest thing in the world dashes against and overcomes the
s: The softest thing in the world dashes against and overcomes the hardest. That which has no substantial existence enters where there is no crevice. The speaker says this shows the advantage of doing nothing with a purpose. Few in the world attain to the teaching without words and the advantage arising from non-action.

l: the softest thing, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 43. 1. The softest thing in the world dashes against and overcomes the
s: It dashes against and overcomes the hardest.

l: the hardest, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 43. 1. The softest thing in the world dashes against and overcomes the
s: It is dashed against and overcome by the softest thing.

l: the teaching without words, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 43. 1. The softest thing in the world dashes against and overcomes the
s: Few in the world attain to it.

l: freedom from action and purpose, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 43. 1. The softest thing in the world dashes against and overcomes the
s: The speaker knows its advantage through the softest thing overcoming the hardest and that which has no substantial existence entering where there is no crevice.

l: non-action, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 43. 1. The softest thing in the world dashes against and overcomes the
s: An advantage arises from it.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 44.
s: The unit compares fame, life, and wealth, asking which a person should value most. It argues that keeping life while giving up fame and wealth avoids greater sorrow and pain. It teaches that pursuing fame or large stores means rejecting greater riches, while contentment and knowing when to stop protect a person from shame, blame, and danger.

l: fame, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 44.
s: Fame is presented as something a person may value over life, but cleaving to fame means rejecting what is more great. Pursuing fame can bring sorrow and pain nearer.

l: life, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 44.
s: Life is presented as more valuable than fame and wealth. Keeping life while losing the other things is said to avoid greater sorrow and pain, and a person who lives contentedly and knows when to stop may live long.

l: wealth, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 44.
s: Wealth is presented as something a person may value over life, but loving large stores means giving up the richer state. Pursuing wealth can bring sorrow and pain nearer.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 45.
s: The unit states that a person who considers great achievements poor will preserve vigour for a long time.
